_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden party-architect). PARTY ARCHITECT REWRITE INSTRUCTIONS pass, 2026-09-05: full schema replacement. Old schema (energy_curve, mixing_strategies, conversation_starters, food_and_drink_strategy, music_plan, the_exit, budget_breakdown, disaster_prevention) is GONE — do not resurrect those keys. New: event_read{what_matters,design_priority}, event_shape (pacing STRATEGY, never a feelings prediction), timeline[]{time,phase,action,host_job,why,adjust_if} with RELATIVE time offsets only (Arrival/+20 min/Around halfway/Final 45 min — never a clock time, since this form collects no start time), helping_people_connect[] (was mixing_strategies, 0-3, no forced count), conversation_catalysts[] (0-3), food_and_drink{format,timing,dietary_considerations,special_touch} (dietary_considerations must be procedural — 'identify/separate/label' — never a safety ASSURANCE like 'will keep guests safe'), music{show,arrival,later,wind_down} (show=false + empty fields when irrelevant), budget_priorities{approach,protect_spending_on[],keep_secondary[],use_what_you_have[]} (priorities, never a fabricated total or a 'budget is workable' verdict), things_to_plan_for[] (was disaster_prevention, 0-4, grounded only in supplied facts, never a predicted future event), wind_down{signals[],script} (top-level — DIFFERENT from music.wind_down, which is about lowering volume). Uses router.outputStandard='v2' + runOutputGuard (prohibit/require list) instead of the old bare toArray()-coerce with no guard. IMPORTANT GOTCHA FIXED THIS PASS: the guard's own repair sometimes blanks a flagged field to '' when it can't produce a clean rewrite (observed live on conversation_catalysts and budget_priorities.protect_spending_on) — outputGuard's requiredNonEmpty only protects a fixed known-in-advance path, not a dynamically-indexed array item, so party-architect.js adds its own pruneEmpties() pass AFTER the guard to drop any blanked plain-string array item or object-array item whose primary field (how/plan/action+host_job) came back blank. DO NOT remove pruneEmpties — it is the only thing standing between a guard repair and a visible blank line/empty bullet in production. Case 1 (housewarming) is a guard PASS with zero violations on this run — case 2 (40th birthday) exercises a guard FAIL-then-repair cycle (7 fields, all successfully rewritten with real content, none needed pruning on this particular run, but the dietary_considerations field is the reference for the 'never a safety assurance' fix — compare it against the pre-fix version in git history, which said a labeling setup 'will keep guests safe'). Frontend Recent Plans is a NEW store (`party-plans`, full inputs+plan+date) — the old `party-history` store (preview-only) stays read-only/legacy, same migration pattern as Small Change Big Difference's Recent Small Changes.

input.whoIsComing: Three couples from my old job, my brother, and the neighbours from downstairs who I have spoken to twice. Nobody knows anybody outside their own pair.
input.space: One-bed flat. Living room seats five if two people take the floor. Kitchen is a corridor. No outdoor space.
input.constraints: Building has a noise rule after 10pm and thin floors. Nine people is already more than the room comfortably holds.

helping_people_connect.how: When each pair arrives, bring them into the room and introduce them to whoever is already there with one specific, neutral detail — what they do, how you know them, or something about the occasion. You do not need to manufacture connections; just make the introduction so nobody is left guessing.
helping_people_connect.when: Each time a new pair arrives, in the first third of the gathering.
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: With nobody knowing anyone outside their own pair, a quick host introduction removes the awkwardness of strangers working out whether to speak first — especially useful in a small flat where people cannot easily drift to a separate area.

helping_people_connect.how: Offer a brief, informal tour of the flat early on — even a one-bed does not take long. Walk a small cluster through it, pointing out anything you are genuinely pleased with or still figuring out. Guests from different pairs who join the same tour have something immediate to react to together.
helping_people_connect.when: Once a few people have arrived, before the room feels settled.
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: A housewarming gives the space itself a natural reason to be the subject of conversation, and a tour creates movement in a room that cannot easily absorb nine people standing in one spot.

conversation_catalysts: If you have a shelf, sideboard, or windowsill with a few objects that tell a story about the move or the flat — a photo, something you unpacked last, something you have not found a home for yet — leave it visible and slightly imperfect. An unfinished corner of a new home invites comment without requiring any setup.

If you already have photos from different periods of your life displayed or easily accessible, a small grouping somewhere other than behind the main seating gives people a reason to wander over and ask questions.

A sign or handwritten note on the fridge or counter saying something like 'help yourself' lowers the friction of guests navigating an unfamiliar kitchen corridor and gives the neighbours in particular — who know you least — a clear signal they are genuinely welcome to move around.

food_and_drink.format: Grazing — a mix of finger food and small bites set out on a counter or coffee table rather than a sit-down spread. With nine people and seating for five, a grazing format makes it easier for guests to move around than assigned or plate-based eating, which tends to fix people in one spot for longer than the space can comfortably absorb.
food_and_drink.timing: Put food out when the first guests arrive so it is already there as people settle in, rather than appearing mid-party. This removes a 'waiting' phase and gives early arrivals something to do. If you want a small shared food moment — bringing out a dessert or a final item — that works well roughly two-thirds of the way through as a natural gathering point before the wind-down.
food_and_drink.dietary_considerations: No dietary needs were supplied. If any come up before the event, identify which dishes contain or may contain the relevant allergens, keep those in separate serving dishes with their own utensils, and label them clearly.
food_and_drink.special_touch: A self-serve drinks station — even a tray with a few options, a bucket of ice, and a jug of something non-alcoholic alongside whatever else you are offering — means guests can help themselves without asking, which matters when the kitchen is a corridor and you cannot easily be behind the counter all evening.

music.arrival: Something familiar and low-attention — choose whatever you genuinely listen to that fits a relaxed mood and is quiet enough that people do not raise their voices to be heard. The goal at arrival is that music is present without being noticed.
music.later: If the room feels like it could handle slightly more energy in the second hour, nudge the volume up a little and shift to tracks with a bit more rhythm within the same general feel — no genre jump needed.
music.wind_down: Lower the volume noticeably in the final half-hour rather than relying on music alone to signal the end of the evening. Quieter music supports the room settling naturally without creating an abrupt shift.

budget_priorities.approach: With $120 for nine people in a grazing format, protect what goes in front of guests first — food and drink for the evening — and treat everything else as secondary. A well-stocked drinks tray and a few generous grazing plates will do more for the gathering than anything decorative.
protect_spending_on: Food for nine people across roughly three hours of grazing — enough that the spread does not look bare by the second hour.
A solid non-alcoholic option and at least one other drink choice, so the self-serve tray works for everyone.
Ice, serving dishes, and napkins if you do not already have what you need — these are easy to underestimate.
keep_secondary: Decorative items — a new flat with your own things in it is already the point of a housewarming.
Anything single-use and disposable beyond what is genuinely necessary for the evening.
use_what_you_have: If you already have lamps or string lights, use them instead of buying anything — soft lighting in a small flat does more than most purchased decorations.
If you have a playlist you already listen to, use it rather than building something new.
If you have serving boards, trays, or bowls you own, those are all you need — grazing food does not require matched tableware.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Nine people in a one-bed flat with seating for five.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Decide before anyone arrives where you want people to be able to sit or perch — floor cushions, a dining chair moved to the living room, or a cleared section of floor with a blanket. Having that figured out means you are not improvising with guests already in the room.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Noise rule after 10pm and thin floors.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Know roughly what time you want the gathering to start winding down, and give yourself a buffer before the noise threshold — so you are not relying on guests reading the signal at the last minute. Lowering the music volume is one part of that; a natural closing moment, like a final round of drinks or the dessert beat, gives you something to point to rather than having to ask people to leave.

things_to_plan_for.issue: The downstairs neighbours are guests, which removes one usual buffer.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Worth keeping in mind that the people most likely to be affected by any noise are in the room — which is mostly a good thing, but also means you cannot rely on 'they are not home tonight.' Keep the noise rule in view as the evening progresses.

Set up the drinks and food in the living room or wherever has the most space before anyone arrives, so the kitchen is not a bottleneck all evening. If guests need to go to the kitchen for anything, make it easy to know what they are allowed to help themselves to.

event_read.what_matters: Nine people in a one-bed flat where nobody knows anyone outside their own pair means the room will feel full and the pairings will be obvious — the design should make it easy for people to step out of their pair without it feeling like an effort. The neighbours are the only guests without a work connection to you, so they are the one pair worth a deliberate early introduction.
event_read.design_priority: Keep the physical space from feeling like a bottleneck, and give people reasons to move and talk rather than park in one spot for three hours.

output.event_shape: Start loosely — arrivals staggered in a full flat need a simple landing spot, not an activity. Once everyone is in, one shared moment (a brief house tour or a toast) gives all nine people a common reference point without requiring anyone to perform. The long middle stays open: food, drinks, and conversation do the work. The final stretch simplifies — food away, music quieter, pace slowing — so the end arrives naturally rather than abruptly.

timeline.action: Drinks station ready and self-serve. Snacks out and accessible without anyone needing to ask. Designate floor cushions or a cleared corner so it is obvious where extra people can sit comfortably.
timeline.host_job: Open the door, hand people a drink if they need help finding it, and point the neighbours toward your work friends with a one-line connection — 'these are my downstairs neighbours, they have lived here longer than I have.' Then step back.
timeline.why: A self-serve setup means you are not pouring drinks for nine people while also welcoming them. The early introduction to the neighbours reduces the chance they spend the whole evening only talking to each other.

timeline.action: Once the last guests have had a few minutes to settle, offer a quick tour of the flat — living room to bedroom to kitchen, two minutes at most. Frame it as the actual point of a housewarming: showing people the place.
timeline.host_job: Lead the tour casually. It naturally moves nine people through the space, breaks up any fixed seating, and gives everyone something to react to together.
timeline.why: A tour is the one activity that is native to a housewarming, requires no setup, and briefly makes everyone part of the same moment without feeling forced. It also resets where people are standing, which can open up new conversations.
timeline.adjust_if: If the room is already relaxed and mixing well, skip the tour — it is not worth interrupting something that is already working.

timeline.action: Bring out the main food. Nothing new needs to happen — this is the longest stretch of the evening and it should feel like it.
timeline.host_job: Eat, talk, enjoy yourself. Refill things when they run low. You do not need to manage the room.
timeline.why: Food gives people a reason to move to the kitchen doorway, shift seats, and change who they are talking to — without any of that being staged.

timeline.host_job: Check that drinks are still available. Otherwise, stay in the room and be a guest at your own party.
timeline.why: The middle of a relaxed gathering does not need an intervention. Holding off on any new moves keeps the later wind-down from feeling rushed.

timeline.action: Bring out something small and sweet — a box of chocolates, a simple dessert, whatever fits the budget. Begin clearing main food dishes from the table.
timeline.host_job: Lower the music slightly if it has drifted up. Clearing dishes is a natural, non-pointed signal that the meal portion is over.
timeline.why: A small sweet course marks a transition without announcing one. Tidying the table shifts the room's feel without anyone being told the party is ending.

timeline.action: No new food, no new music choices. Let the room quiet on its own.
timeline.host_job: Say the wind-down line when a natural pause arrives. Do not wait for everyone to leave simultaneously — walk the first people to the door warmly and the rest will follow.
timeline.why: The noise rule gives you a real, external reason to close the evening — use it plainly rather than engineering an atmosphere.

signals: Stop bringing out new food or drinks and begin consolidating what is left onto one tray or area.
Lower the music to a level where it is clearly background rather than atmosphere.
Mention the building noise rule naturally — it is a real constraint and a completely honest reason to wrap up.
wind_down.script: This has been such a good evening — thank you all for coming to see the place. I do have to keep an eye on the building noise rule, so I am going to start winding things down, but I am really glad you are all here.

input.whoIsComing: Mostly close friends from the last 15 years, a few work people, 3 kids under 10. About a third haven't met each other.
input.space: Backyard with covered patio, fits ~25 standing. Kitchen and living room flow out to it. Late September — should be warm but cool by 9pm.
input.constraints: Two guests have tree nut allergies, one is gluten-free, one is sober (they're fine with others drinking).

helping_people_connect.how: In the first 30-40 minutes, greet people as they arrive and introduce them by name to others you see standing alone or in small clusters. If you know two people have something in common, mention it; otherwise, a simple introduction and then stepping back is enough to break the ice.
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: A named introduction removes the awkward opening and gives people a reason to keep talking rather than standing alone.

helping_people_connect.how: Place drinks in one spot and food in another — both accessible but not the same table — so guests have a natural reason to move between areas rather than staying planted in one cluster.
helping_people_connect.when: Set up before guests arrive; maintain throughout
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: Placing drinks in one spot and food in another means guests have to move between areas to get what they want, which naturally breaks up static clusters and creates reasons for people to cross paths.

conversation_catalysts: If you have photos from the last 15 years, set up a small display near the entrance or on a patio surface. Guests who know the subject can point things out; guests who do not have something to ask about.

A low-key birthday sign-in or note card for guests to write a short memory or wish gives the birthday person something to read later and gives arriving guests a small, optional thing to do while the room is still filling.

food_and_drink.format: Grazing with a central food table — not plated, not assigned seating. A grazing setup makes it easier for guests to move around than a served or sit-down format, which fits a mixed group at a relaxed backyard party.
food_and_drink.timing: Have food ready and visible when the first guests arrive so there is something to do immediately. If you plan a cake or dessert moment, hold it for roughly the midpoint of the evening — it creates a natural pause and gives everyone a shared moment regardless of how the conversations have split.
food_and_drink.dietary_considerations: Identify which dishes contain or may contain tree nuts, keep those in separate serving dishes with their own utensils, and label them clearly. Do the same for dishes containing gluten, and offer at least two or three items that are naturally gluten-free without modification. Make sure the sober guest has appealing non-alcoholic drink options presented the same way as everything else — not as an afterthought.
food_and_drink.special_touch: A simple non-alcoholic drink that looks like it belongs — a good sparkling water with fresh citrus, or a house mocktail — served in the same glasses as everything else, so the sober guest is not quietly handed something different.

music.arrival: Familiar, low-key background music at a volume where people do not have to raise their voices — something that fits the relaxed vibe you have in mind. Let conversation be the main sound.
music.later: If the energy picks up and you want the room to feel livelier, raise the volume slightly and shift toward something a little more rhythmic — staying in the same general territory so it does not feel like a genre change.
music.wind_down: Lower the volume gradually rather than switching to something noticeably quieter; the goal is to soften the room, not signal anything.

budget_priorities.approach: With 22 adults and 3 children across four hours, food and drink for the full guest count is where the budget works hardest and where cutting shows most. Everything else is secondary to that.
protect_spending_on: Food and drink sufficient for the guest count, including good non-alcoholic options and enough variety to accommodate the dietary needs you have described.
Any weather or comfort gear the outdoor space actually needs for late September — a heat source or blankets for when the temperature drops around 9pm.
keep_secondary: Decorations beyond what you already own.
Entertainment or activities beyond what the gathering itself provides.
use_what_you_have: If you already have string lights, outdoor lamps, or candles, use them — they do more for late-evening outdoor ambiance than most purchased decor.
If you have a Bluetooth speaker that covers the patio well, no additional audio setup is necessary.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Temperature drop late in the evening
things_to_plan_for.plan: You noted the space will cool by 9pm. Decide ahead whether you will have blankets or a clear, comfortable indoor overflow space so guests are not caught off guard if the temperature drops.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Children under 10 in a primarily adult gathering
things_to_plan_for.plan: Decide whether the kids will move freely through the main gathering or whether a designated spot — a corner of the indoor space with something to occupy them — would make it easier on their parents and on the flow of adult conversation.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Tree nut allergies and shared serving setup
things_to_plan_for.plan: Plan your serving layout before guests arrive: identify every dish that contains or may contain tree nuts, assign those their own serving utensils, and label them so guests can identify them without having to ask.

At 22 guests plus 3 children, you are near your covered patio's stated limit. Make sure the kitchen and living room are genuinely accessible and not blocked by furniture or bags, so overflow is easy and natural rather than crowded.

event_read.what_matters: With a third of guests who haven't met and three kids in the mix, the main design challenge is giving unfamiliar adults easy ways to connect without turning a relaxed birthday into a structured event. The cooling temperature late in the evening is the one environmental factor worth planning around.
event_read.design_priority: Keep the host free to be present as the birthday person's guest-of-honor friend, not a stage manager — structure just enough to remove friction, then let the gathering run itself.

output.event_shape: Start loosely so arrivals feel natural and nobody walks into a moment already in progress. Let the first half be mostly open — food out, drinks accessible, people finding their footing. Add one shared birthday moment roughly halfway through, which gives unfamiliar guests a common reference point without requiring anyone to perform. After that, keep it open and easy until the temperature or the hour prompts a natural close.

timeline.action: Food and drinks are already out and accessible — guests can serve themselves immediately. Kids have a designated spot with something to do so parents can settle in.
timeline.host_job: Greet people at the door, point out the drink setup and bathrooms, and make one or two introductions when you genuinely know two people will have something to talk about. Then step back.
timeline.why: Self-serve from the start means guests are not waiting on the host and the host is not running food. Arrivals stretch — this absorbs that without anyone missing anything.

timeline.action: Nothing new — food is still out, conversation is moving. If a few guests clearly haven't connected to anyone yet, this is the window for a low-key introduction.
timeline.host_job: Check that food is stocked and the tree-nut-labeled dishes are still clearly separated with their own utensils. Otherwise, be a guest.
timeline.why: By this point, arrivals have slowed and people have had time to settle in. Continue stocking the food and introduce any arrivals to someone already in conversation if the moment feels natural.

timeline.action: Bring out the birthday cake or dessert with candles. Keep it short — gather people, song, candles, done. No speeches required unless someone wants to give one.
timeline.host_job: Initiate the gather ('Hey everyone, cake time') and then step aside — let it happen around the birthday person.
timeline.why: A single shared moment gives the whole room — including guests who haven't met — something in common to react to. It also marks the midpoint naturally without announcing it.
timeline.adjust_if: If the room is deep in conversation and the moment feels like an interruption, push it 15-20 minutes and wait for a natural lull.

timeline.action: Dessert stays out. Main food can begin to consolidate — cover or put away anything that has been sitting a while. Music continues at the same level.
timeline.host_job: Tidy the food table lightly, refill what needs refilling, then return to the party. No new activities needed.
timeline.why: Consolidating food signals the event is past its midpoint without saying so, and reduces the host's cleanup load at the end.

timeline.action: Lower the music volume one step. Stop introducing new food. If it has cooled down, this is when guests naturally move toward the warmer indoor space — let that happen without directing it.
timeline.host_job: Begin slow, visible cleanup of the patio — stacking plates, consolidating cups. This is a natural, non-pushy signal that the end is near.
timeline.why: Lowering the music volume and clearing the food table are visible signals that the event is winding down. Guests can read these cues without being told.
timeline.adjust_if: If the room is still lively and no one seems ready to leave, hold off on cleanup and give it another 15 minutes.

timeline.action: Guests begin saying goodbyes naturally. Keep some drinks and dessert available for anyone lingering.
timeline.host_job: Say a brief closing line when there's a natural pause, and walk departing guests to the door.
timeline.why: A short, warm closing signal removes ambiguity about whether the party is over, without cutting off anyone still enjoying themselves.

signals: Stop bringing out new food and consolidate what remains onto one table.
Lower the music volume gradually over the final stretch.
Begin a light, visible tidy of the serving area.
wind_down.script: Thank you all so much for coming out tonight — it's meant a lot having everyone here. I'm going to start winding things down, but please don't rush off.
